idiom_name: final class conforming to the protocol, flag guarded by a lock
implementation_notes: Swift has no proxy objects, so the forwarder is a final class that conforms to the target's protocol and holds the target plus a revocation flag: each protocol requirement checks the flag and forwards, or throws. It must be a class - a struct would copy the flag, so revocation on the grantor's copy would not affect the collaborator's - and the flag needs a lock or an atomic because grants are used across threads. Hold the target weakly when the grant should not extend the target's lifetime; the protocol then has to be class-bound for weak to apply.
pitfalls: A struct (or actor) forwarder changes the semantics: value types copy the flag so revocation misses copies, and an actor serialises every forwarded call through its executor, which couples revocation to the actor's queue.

Throwing from a protocol requirement only works where the requirement declares throws; for non-throwing requirements pick a failure channel (fatalError, a Result-returning facade, or a policy object) instead of a silent no-op.
Holding the target strongly keeps it alive past revocation, and capturing the wrapper in a target callback creates a cycle unless the target reference is weak.

variants.name: Foundation NSProxy with message forwarding
variants.implementation_notes: On Apple platforms Foundation's NSProxy is the runtime-forwarding alternative: NSProxy is an abstract root class that stands in for another object and raises on any message it does not respond to, so a concrete subclass overrides methodSignatureForSelector: and forwardInvocation: to check the revocation flag and then pass the invocation to the target. This variant works only for Objective-C message sends (it is unavailable on non-Darwin Swift), and it is the closest thing to the dynamic proxies of the JVM and .NET.
pitfalls: NSProxy does not inherit from NSObject, so it has none of NSObject's methods or conformances - a wrapper whose contract is a Swift protocol is normally written as an ordinary class instead.

Messages that NSProxy itself implements (alloc, class, responds(to:)) never reach forwardInvocation, and forwarding failures turn into NSInvalidArgumentException/doesNotRecognizeSelector crashes rather than Swift errors.
